lessons.title: رأس (raʾs) — the head
lessons.gloss: the head — a Semitic root cognate with Hebrew rosh, and the source of "president" in Arabic itself

segments.text: One more ancient Semitic root — and a word still hard at work in modern political vocabulary, the same way Latin's caput is in English.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — The word

segments.text: رأس (raʾs) = "head" — an ancient Semitic root, cousin of Hebrew ראש (rosh), the very word inside Rosh Hashanah, "head of the year."

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — From "head" to "president"

segments.text: Arabic builds رئيس (raʾīs), "president, chief, head [of an organization]," directly on this same root — literally "the one who is the head." That's exactly the move English makes with Latin caput: captain ("head" of a unit), capital ("head" city). Different language families, the same very human idea — the person or place "at the head" is the one in charge.

What does رأس mean, and what's its Hebrew cousin? ("Head" — cousin of rosh, as in Rosh Hashanah.) What word is built on it for "president," and what does it literally mean? (رئيس raʾīs, "the head [one]" — the same "head = leader" idea as English captain/capital from Latin caput.)

lessons.title: يد (yad) — the hand
lessons.gloss: the hand — an ancient Semitic root, nearly unchanged since its Hebrew cousin

segments.text: Some words wear their age lightly — worn down, reshaped, disguised. This one hasn't changed much at all.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — The word

segments.text: يد (yad) = "hand" — a short, ancient Semitic root. Its Hebrew cousin is spelled and pronounced almost identically: יד (yad). Where raʾs/rosh show a family resemblance, yad/yad is closer to twins — one of the more strikingly unchanged shared words across the whole Semitic family.

segments.instruction: the Hebrew twin — "yad" — almost the same word
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the Hebrew twin — "yad" — almost the same word]
[YOU SAY: contrast — "raʾs/rosh" changed more than "yad/yad" did]

segments.text: What does يد mean? ("Hand.") How does it compare to its Hebrew cousin? (Nearly identical — both yad — one of the more strikingly unchanged shared words across the Semitic family.)

lessons.title: How are you, cold
lessons.gloss: the wellbeing exchange run cold — a question that asks after your state rather than after you, a root that means to turn, and two answers where English has one

segments.text: Ask after somebody and answer them back, both parts, without reading on. If the question came out as a memorised noise rather than three pieces you can name, this page is for you.

utterances: word: كيف kayfa. letters, right to left: kāf, yāʾ, fāʾ. what it is: how — a question word, partner to ما.
word: حال ḥāl. letters, right to left: ḥāʾ, alif, lām. what it is: state, condition — root ḥ–w–l, to turn.

segments.text: The ح is the deep throat ḥ, not an English h. And حال is the whole point of the question: English asks after you, Arabic asks after your state — the thing that turns and changes, which is exactly what its root means.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the same suffix, one lesson on

segments.text: كيف حالك؟ bolts three pieces you already own together: how + state + your. The suffix behaves identically to the one that gave you اسمي, and it splits the same way.

utterances: to a man: كيف حالك؟ kayfa ḥāluka. to a woman: كيف حالك؟ kayfa ḥāluki.

segments.text: Literally: how — your-state. No is, no are. The same zero copula that ran through the name exchange runs through this one.

blocks.title: How to answer: two replies where English has one

segments.text: بخير bi-khayr is بـ (in) plus خير (khayr, good) — literally in goodness. You had met khayr long before you were told: it sits inside the morning greeting صباح الخير, morning of the good.

الحمد لله al-ḥamdu lillāh comes back more often than bi-khayr does. Every letter in it is one you can write — alif, lām, ḥāʾ, mīm, dāl, hāʾ — and it says the praise is to God, from the root ḥ–m–d, to praise.

segments.instruction: the three attaching pieces inside these lines — al-, bi-, li-
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the three attaching pieces inside these lines — *al-*, *bi-*, *li-*]

segments.text: Give the root behind حال and what it means. (ḥ–w–l, to turn or change.) Give the literal sense of بخير. (In goodness.) Give the literal sense of الحمد لله. (The praise is to God.) And name the question word that partners كيف. (ما.)
